video_title: Market Call: Kim Bolton's outlook on Technology Stocks (June 10, 2026)
gist: Kim Bolton of Black Swan Dexterity, on a BNN Bloomberg Market Call viewer call-in show hosted by Matt, says he is running a ~52% hedge and ~15% cash into an ongoing big-tech selloff and argues the AI stack's software layer has been captured by private inference companies (Anthropic, OpenAI, Perplexity), leaving application-software names like ServiceNow, Spotify, Adobe and Intuit derated. He works name by name through Canadian and US tech (Xanadu, Celestica, Shopify, Microsoft, Apple, Snowflake, Arista, Veritiv) with price targets and tranche levels, and names ARM Holdings, IBM and Tesla as top picks.

insights.claim: Black Swan Dexterity is carrying roughly a 52% hedge across most portfolios plus about 15% cash, built by shorting equity indexes and buying puts financed by calls sold earlier.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: A technology-dedicated manager at a >50% hedge is a real positioning signal: dip-buying flows from this cohort are unlikely until the hedge comes off.
insights.quote: WE'VE GOT ABOUT A 52% HEDGE ACROSS MOST OF OUR, OUR PORTFOLIOS. WE BUILT UP SOME CASH TO AROUND 15%.

insights.claim: Bolton frames the hard part of hedging as the exit, not the entry — the payoff is decided by when the hedge is removed, not by putting it on.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: A reusable discipline for anyone hedging a drawdown: pre-plan the unwind level, because a well-timed hedge badly removed still loses the upside.
insights.quote: WHERE THE RUBBER HITS THE ROAD IS GOING TO BE WHEN WE TAKE OUR HEDGE OFF.

insights.claim: Bolton flags 28,200 on the futures as the critical support level after they fell there and bounced to around 28,600; a break through it opens roughly another 1,000 points of downside.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: A concrete, falsifiable level to watch for whether the tech pullback becomes a deeper leg down.
insights.quote: IF IT GOES THROUGH THERE, WE'RE PROBABLY GOING DOWN CLOSE TO ANOTHER 1000 POINTS.

insights.claim: Bolton reads the big-tech pullback as a classic post-melt-up unwind that likely has further to run, driven by rebalancing and unusually high macro uncertainty rather than a single catalyst.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Argues against immediately buying the first dip in mega-cap tech, and for treating the drawdown as a two-sided trading opportunity.
insights.quote: SORT OF A CLASSIC CLIMB THAT WALL OF WORRY AND THEN TAKE THE ELEVATOR DOWN.

insights.claim: Bolton's shop applies a hard rule that any position down 15% triggers a full re-examination of the investment thesis, which is how they exited Adobe before its worst decline.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: A transferable stop-and-review discipline that converted a thesis break in software into a realized gain instead of a large loss.
insights.quote: WE ALWAYS HAVE SORT OF A RULE OF THUMB IF WE HAVE A POSITION AND IT GOES SOUTH BY 15%, WE GOT TO REVISIT THE WHOLE INVESTMENT THESIS.

themes.theme: Software derating vs. private inference AI

insights.claim: Bolton argues the software layer of the AI stack has been captured by the private inference companies — Anthropic, OpenAI and Perplexity — rather than by incumbent application-software vendors, a shift he dates to roughly the fall of 2025.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Explains why owning listed application software as an AI proxy has failed, and reframes the AI software trade as one only accessible via IPOs or private markets.
insights.quote: THE INFERENCE SOFTWARE COMPANIES OUT THERE, LIKE THE ANTHROPIC'S AND THE OPEN AI AND THE PERPLEXITIES, THEY, THEY WERE GOING TO BE THE CHOSEN ONES FOR THAT SOFTWARE AI STACK.

insights.claim: Bolton expects the moat now enjoyed by Anthropic, OpenAI and Perplexity to erode once they list publicly, because public-company constraints limit what they can do relative to private status.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Implies the competitive advantage of the AI leaders is partly a private-market artifact — a reason to fade post-IPO enthusiasm and revisit beaten-down incumbents.
insights.quote: THEY HAVE A NICE LITTLE MOAT AROUND IT RIGHT NOW THAT I THINK THAT MOAT WILL DISAPPEAR ONCE THEY GO PUBLIC THOUGH.

insights.claim: Bolton says Microsoft, Meta and IBM have all been marked down simply for carrying software exposure, which he considers an indiscriminate penalty given their consumer, enterprise and government-services businesses.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Frames a mispricing: hardware-plus-software hybrids derated on a sector label rather than fundamentals is where he is buying.
insights.quote: MICROSOFT, META, IBM, THEY'VE ALL SORT OF GOTTEN BEATEN DOWN BECAUSE THEY GET PAINTED WITH THAT SOFTWARE BRUSH.

insights.claim: Bolton dates software's great run to roughly 2010 through 2025 and says the pendulum has swung away from it and will not swing back soon, despite analysts still carrying high price targets on the group.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Warns that large gaps between price and consensus targets in software are a value trap rather than an entry signal.
insights.quote: THEY DID REALLY, REALLY WELL FOR THEMSELVES, YOU KNOW, FROM ABOUT 2010 TO 2025. BUT THEN THE PENDULUM SWUNG. I DON'T THINK IT'S ACTUALLY GOING TO SWING BACK TOWARD THE SOFTWARE VERY SOON.

insights.claim: Bolton expects hardware companies whose stocks have run hard to start acquiring beaten-down software companies in the second half of 2026 or the first half of 2027 in order to broaden out.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Sets up a potential M&A-driven re-rating in derated software names, and a specific window to position for takeout candidates.
insights.quote: I WOULD IMAGINE A LOT OF THESE HARDWARE COMPANIES WHOSE STOCKS HAVE DONE EXTREMELY, EXTREMELY WELL WILL BE VERY ENTICED TO ACTUALLY LOOK AT SOME OF THESE SOFTWARE COMPANIES TO SORT OF BROADEN OUT.

insights.claim: Spotify was Bolton's June 18 top pick a year ago on the thesis that software would monetize AI hardware, and it is down about 30% since; he realised between mid-September and mid-October 2025 that inference-AI competitors would absorb the attention, and now cites it at about $500 versus a $605 12-month target with 800 million paying subscribers and a $105 billion market cap.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: A worked example that scale and subscriber moats did not protect application software from the inference-AI attention shift — check that thesis before buying other 'AI-enabled' consumer platforms.

insights.claim: Bolton exited Roblox at the beginning of October 2025 for about a 10% loss and would not touch it now at roughly $42 despite a $65 12-month price target, because inference-AI entrants undercut its 3D digital-worlds story.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Signals he treats the AI-native disruption of engagement platforms as structural, not a dip to buy, even with a 50%+ implied upside to consensus.
insights.quote: ROBLOX RIGHT NOW $42, 12 MONTH PRICE TARGET IS 65. OKAY, BUT I WOULDN'T TOUCH IT.

insights.claim: Bolton treats a CEO departure as a thesis-killer, citing Adobe's CEO quitting after the stock's spike as the reason he is glad not to hold it despite a $327 average 12-month target and $105 billion market cap.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: A quick qualitative filter for derated software: management conviction is the tell, and a big analyst-target gap does not offset it.
insights.quote: THEN THE CEO QUIT. AND LIKE, IF THE CEO LOSES FAITH, WHAT HAVE YOU GOT?

insights.claim: Bolton says Anthropic is reportedly slated to go public in July and warns against buying the heavily subscribed inference-AI IPOs coming to market, arguing better entry points will come later.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Actionable stance for the coming AI listing wave: skip the allocation scramble and wait for post-lockup or post-hype pricing.
insights.quote: I THINK IT'S SORT OF DANGEROUS GETTING INTO THESE HEAVILY SUBSCRIBED INFERENCE AI IPOS THAT ARE GOING TO BE COMING UP. YOU'LL HAVE LOTS OF OPPORTUNITY LATER.

insights.claim: Bolton notes OpenAI's CEO publicly acknowledged that going public removes freedoms the company had while private, and reads the whole cohort as motivated to monetize a decade of spending.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Supports the view that listing itself changes the competitive behaviour of the AI leaders — the key variable behind his moat-erosion call.
insights.quote: ONCE YOU BECOME PUBLIC, THERE ARE A LOT OF THINGS YOU CAN'T DO THAT YOU COULD DO WHEN YOU WERE PRIVATE.

insights.claim: Bolton owns a one-third position in Xanadu, a pure-play Canadian photonic quantum computing company, with a 12-month price target of $60.15 against a share price around $17, and plans to add another third near $16.25.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: A specific accumulation level and an unusually wide target-to-price gap in a listed pure-play quantum name.
insights.quote: WE'VE GOT A 12 MONTH PRICE TARGET OF $60.15.

insights.claim: Bolton's Xanadu case rests on its open-source PennyLane software stack, a collaboration with Oak Ridge National Laboratory, and its introduction of what he calls the world's first modular networked photonic quantum computer.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Identifies the concrete validation milestones — a national-lab partnership and a software ecosystem — that separate a fundable quantum story from a concept stock.

insights.claim: Bolton took profits in Celestica last week near the tech top and would re-enter just under $500, adding at $475 and $450, against a 12-month price target of $650.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: A named re-entry ladder in the Canadian AI-hardware bellwether, with earnings due at the beginning of July as the next catalyst.
insights.quote: WE HAVE A 12 MONTH PRICE TARGET OF 650 AND WE TOOK THE PROFIT JUST LAST WEEK.

insights.claim: Bolton would buy Shopify here in tranches, holding it in some separately managed accounts, citing an average 12-month price target of C$190 to C$195 and a roughly $200 billion market cap, and says its downtrend looks near a bottom.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: One of the few software-brushed names he is buying rather than avoiding, on the argument the derating has largely run its course.
insights.quote: WHAT THAT REALLY SORT OF TELLS ME IS THAT IT'S GETTING NEAR THE BOTTOM.

insights.claim: Bolton points to Constellation Software rallying from about 2,400 to nearly 3,000 in a month as evidence that selective bargains still exist inside the derated software group.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Qualifies his bearish software call — the derating is not uniform, so dispersion within software is tradeable.
insights.quote: IT WAS ONLY A MONTH AGO THAT CONSTELLATION SOFTWARE WAS DOWN AT 2400, AND NOW IT'S UP ALMOST AT 3000.

insights.claim: Bolton does not own Apply Digital and classifies it as a trading vehicle rather than an investment, suggesting picking it up between 30 and 35 with it near 40 and letting it run above 40.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: A chart-based range trade rather than a holding — useful distinction for sizing small-cap Canadian tech exposure.
insights.quote: IT'S IT'S MORE OF A TRADING STOCK RATHER THAN AN INVESTMENT STOCK.

insights.claim: Bolton sells one- and two-week calls on his Apple position every time the stock approaches $300 to harvest premium, because at about $291 versus a $316 average 12-month target the runway is thin.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: A concrete way to keep owning a fully valued mega-cap: convert a low expected return into recurring income at a known strike.
insights.quote: EVERY TIME IT GETS UP SORT OF AROUND THAT $300 LEVEL, WE'VE BEEN SELLING SORT OF ONE AND TWO WEEK CALLS JUST TO EARN SOME, JUST TO EARN SOME, SOME INCOME, SOME PREMIUMS.

insights.claim: For investors drawn to Intuit's $490 analyst target versus a price near $290 after a miserable quarter, Bolton recommends selling puts at a strike you genuinely want to own rather than buying at the market, while saying software is still not the place to be.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Turns a value-trap temptation into a paid-to-wait structure, with the premium as compensation for a thesis he does not endorse.
insights.quote: I'D ACTUALLY SELL SOME PUTS, SELL SOME PUTS WITH A STRIKE PRICE THAT YOU REALLY, REALLY WANT TO OWN IT AT RATHER THAN JUST SORT OF BUY IT AT THE MARKET.

insights.claim: Bolton would write calls against both Flex and Snowflake after their S&P 500 inclusion spikes, rolling strike prices up to avoid being called away rather than selling the shares.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Treats index-inclusion pops as monetizable volatility events rather than durable re-ratings — a repeatable playbook for post-inclusion names.
insights.quote: WHEN IT SORT OF GOT INTO THIS NOSEBLEED AREA, IT'S, IT'S TIME TO WRITE SOME CALLS.

insights.claim: Bolton cites technology vendors accounting for 55% of S&P market cap with the top ten alone at 40%, and compares that front-loading to an ingredient he saw during the dot-com period.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Quantifies why index exposure is now a concentrated tech bet, and flags the historical analogue he is hedging against.
insights.quote: NOW TECHNOLOGY VENDORS ACTUALLY ACCOUNT FOR 55% OF THE MARKET CAP OF THE S&P. AND ACTUALLY THOSE TOP TEN ACCOUNT FOR 40%.

insights.claim: Asked whether to hold the XLT technology ETF, Bolton says a sector ETF behaves like a mutual fund that only works while the market rises and argues investors need an active technology manager who can protect unrealized gains in a drawdown — the opposite of Warren Buffett's advice to just put the money in the S&P.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: A self-interested but explicit case against passive tech exposure at peak concentration; the testable claim is whether hedged active beats the ETF through this correction.
insights.quote: YOU NEED A TECHNOLOGY HEDGE FUND MANAGER THAT CAN ACTUALLY PROTECT, YOU KNOW, YOUR UNREALISED GAINS WHEN THE MARKET STARTS TO CRATER LIKE IT IS RIGHT NOW.

insights.claim: Bolton attributes much of the current market volatility to the Trump regime and says the resulting options and derivatives opportunities on the downside are as large as the opportunities on the way up.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Policy-driven volatility is his stated reason for running a derivatives-heavy book rather than long-only tech.
insights.quote: IT PROBABLY HAS SOMETHING A LOT TO DO WITH THE TRUMP REGIME AND SO ON. THERE'S A LOT OF VOLATILITY.

insights.claim: Bolton likes Veritiv Holdings as a data-center infrastructure play built on power management, thermal management and integrated rack systems, boosted by acquisitions he names as Marco Structures and Thermo Keys, and would buy around $280 and add at $270 and $260 against a $377 average 12-month target on a $155 billion company.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Names the picks-and-shovels layer he is still willing to buy outright, with explicit tranche levels, while hedging the broader tech tape.

insights.claim: Bolton holds a full position in Arista Networks near 152.5 against a 182.5 twelve-month target — about a 20% lift — and would still buy in tranches at 147.5 and 140, having sold calls when it reached 165.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Shows how he combines a full core position with covered-call sales at the top of the range instead of trimming.
insights.quote: ONE OF THE REASONS THAT THEY'VE DONE BETTER THAN CISCO IS BECAUSE THEY DIDN'T HAVE ALL THE LEGACY HARDWARE PRODUCTS THAT CISCO HAD BEFORE.

insights.claim: Bolton owns Snowflake in separately managed accounts and argues it is unfairly caught in the software derating because it is enterprise, not consumer, software sitting inside data centers and cloud networks, trading just under 244 against a 292 average 12-month target with no earnings until August 26.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific mispricing candidate within his own bearish software call, with a long catalyst gap that argues for call-writing in the meantime.
insights.quote: IT HAS A NICE MOAT AROUND IT. IT DOESN'T HAVE A HECK OF A LOT OF COMPETITION.

insights.claim: ARM Holdings is a Bolton top pick at roughly 343 with a 447 twelve-month target, on power-efficient CPU designs that are ubiquitous in smartphones and tablets, SoftBank still the largest shareholder, and optionality from a possible move into fabrication; he is adding here with tranches at 325 and 305.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: A named top pick with explicit entry ladder, and a watch item — any move by ARM from fabless licensing toward fabrication would change its margin profile.
insights.quote: WHERE THEY REALLY CARVED OUT A NICE NICHE IS, IS IN MAKING THEIR, THEIR CHIPS VERY, ESPECIALLY THEIR CPUS, VERY POWER EFFICIENT.

insights.claim: IBM is a Bolton top pick at a full 4.5% position because after spinning off its supercomputer business it combines hardware, software, AI and quantum, with adds planned around 270 and 255 despite an execution slip in the April 22 earnings.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Position sizing (4.5%) plus add levels give a clear read on conviction in a name he admits sounds boring after a six-month high.
insights.quote: THEY'RE BIG ON BIG INTO THE AI. THEY'RE HUGE INTO THE QUANTUM. SO THEY CHECK ALL THE BOXES.

insights.claim: Bolton's Tesla thesis is that batteries have already overtaken electric vehicles in revenue and that the Optimus robotics business will overtake batteries later this year, made possible by vertical integration rather than external supply chains.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: If the revenue mix claim is right, Tesla should be modelled as an energy and robotics company, not an automaker — a materially different multiple.
insights.quote: AN EVEN BIGGER BUSINESS THAN THE ELECTRIC VEHICLES ARE THE BATTERIES. IT'S ACTUALLY OVERTAKEN IT IN REVENUE.

insights.claim: Bolton likes Tesla more at about 385 than at the 410 to 414 level where he first named it a top pick, and says his rule is to buy between 350 and 375 and let it go around 425 to 450, with his own target above the 405 analyst average.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: A defined range-trading band in a high-beta mega-cap, plus a rare case where his target sits above consensus.
insights.quote: WE'VE, WE'VE LEARNED YOU BUY TESLA SORT OF ANYWHERE BETWEEN 350 AND 375 AND YOU LET IT GO UP AT AROUND FOUR AND A QUARTER FOR 50.

insights.claim: Microsoft is in Bolton's top five holdings at just over $400 against a $560 average 12-month analyst target, which he argues understates its consumer, enterprise and government-services positions because it is penalized for its software side.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Roughly 40% implied upside to consensus in a core mega-cap he is holding through the selloff rather than hedging out of.
insights.quote: BECAUSE THEY'RE BOTH A HARDWARE AND A SOFTWARE COMPANY, THEY GET PUT IN THE PENALTY BOX BECAUSE OF THE SOFTWARE SIDE.

insights.claim: Bolton calls Apple's recent developer-conference announcement an anti-climax under a new hardware-focused executive who appeared to be cleaning house, but rates the Siri upgrades using Gemini as very important, and would accumulate around 285 to 280 while doubting it trades much below 275.
insights.speaker: Kim Bolton
insights.so_what: Frames Apple as a fully valued income position, not a growth story, with the Gemini-powered Siri partnership as the variable that could change that.
insights.quote: THE UPGRADES IN SIRI WITH GEMINI ARE VERY, VERY IMPORTANT. IT IS A BIT RICH.
